title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Module 3: the third border cost
text:
Module 3: the third border cost
Distance · currencies · jurisdictions · trade rules
Distance became cheap. The currency broke. Today the border is a legal one, and the firm can choose which side of it to stand on.

A firm cannot easily move its customers or its engineers. It can move where its profit is reported.


Timing: 0–3 minutes. Reconnect to the two previous sessions. The container made distance nearly free, so location was decided by other costs. The baht showed that a border the firm had ignored could destroy it. Today’s border cost is different in kind, because the others were imposed on the firm while this one is partly chosen by it.
Make the framing precise before the readings come in. A multinational is not one legal person. It is a group of separately incorporated companies, each a taxpayer somewhere, bound together by ownership. Transactions between those companies count for tax purposes even though nothing leaves the group.
Note the three readings and what each supplies. Duhigg and Kocieniewski describe the structure as it stood in 2012. The Financial Times reports what a new disclosure rule revealed in 2026. Setser explains why fourteen years of reform left Ireland collecting more than ever.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Apple sold products across Europe, booked the profit in Ireland, and paid very little on most of it. Nothing Duhigg and Kocieniewski describe was shown to break a law. Where should that profit have been taxed, and by whom? Test your answer: name the rule you would write, and say which country loses revenue if it is adopted.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted · No internet or LLMs


Commit to a rule before we reconstruct the structure.


Timing: 3–13 minutes. The second sentence of the prompt does the work. Students will readily say profit should be taxed “where the value is created.” Requiring them to name a rule forces them to discover that every candidate assigns the revenue to a different state, and that no neutral principle picks among them.
Common answers and where each leads: tax where the customer is, which favours large consumer markets and disadvantages small exporting economies; tax where the employees are, which favours the United States and hurts Ireland; tax where the intellectual property is legally owned, which is close to the existing rule and is precisely what the firm chooses; tax at the parent’s residence, which invites the firm to move its headquarters.
Duhigg and Kocieniewski note that the US tax code rests on the idea that a company earns income where value is created rather than where products are sold. Hold that back until a student proposes it, then ask how anyone would locate the creation of a patent.
[Source] - Charles Duhigg and David Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes,” The New York Times, April 28, 2012.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Hypotheses
text:
Hypotheses

Where should the profit be taxed?


Now name the country that loses revenue under your rule.


Timing: 13–17 minutes. Take four or five rules and write each on the board as a short phrase. Do not sort them. Then reveal the second question and work down the list, asking the class rather than the author to name the loser under each rule.
The board list should end up showing that the disagreement is not technical. Each rule is a claim by one state on a tax base that another state also claims. Leave the list standing; you will return to it after the Court of Justice decision and again at the end.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The same move, inside one country
text:
The same move, inside one country



8.84% → 0%


California’s corporate rate, and Nevada’s



In 2006 Apple opened Braeburn Capital in Reno, 200 miles from Cupertino, to hold and invest the company’s cash.

Since then the cash has earned more than $2.5bn in interest and dividends. Nevada charges no corporate income tax and no capital gains tax.

The arrangement also cut what Apple owed in other states, because many reduce the bill when financial management sits elsewhere.



Timing: 17–20 minutes. Start here rather than in Ireland, because the domestic case strips away everything that sounds exotic. There is no foreign country, no treaty, and no currency. There are two US states with different rates and one subsidiary placed in the cheaper one.
Ask the class what Nevada actually supplied. The answer is a rate and a legal address. The engineers, the designers, the executives who decide how to invest the money, and the customers are all somewhere else. Nevada supplied the one scarce input, which was a low rate attached to a place where a company could be said to exist.
Two details reward attention. The reporters note that Braeburn is a variety of apple that is both sweet and tart, and that Baldwin, the name of the Virgin Islands holding company you will meet shortly, is known for travelling well. Someone chose those names. The office itself sits down a narrow hallway across from an abandoned restaurant.
Apple is not unusual here. The article lists Cisco, Harley-Davidson, and Microsoft as also using Nevada subsidiaries, with hundreds more incorporating in Delaware.
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Value is made in many places and reported in one
text:
Value is made in many places and reported in one


Nothing here is illegal. The question is what determines the size of the arrow.


Timing: 20–23 minutes. Walk across the top row and ask where each activity physically sits. Design and engineering in California, components across East Asia and Europe, assembly in China, retail in every market, support in several regional centres.
Then make the accounting point. Each activity is carried out by a separate legal company inside the group, and each must be paid by the others for what it contributes. Those internal payments determine how much profit remains in each country. The group’s worldwide profit is fixed by the market; its distribution across countries is set by prices the group writes for itself.
Do not let students conclude this is merely a fiction. The transactions are governed by contracts, the entities hold real legal rights, and the profits genuinely accrue to them under the law of each jurisdiction. That is exactly why the practice is hard to reach.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Transfer pricing is the price a firm charges itself
text:
Transfer pricing is the price a firm charges itself


The rule
Related companies must transact at the price unrelated companies would have agreed.
Tax authorities call this the arm’s-length principle.

The difficulty
There is no market price for the right to use an iPhone’s design.
The asset is unique, so no comparable transaction exists to check the price against.


The rule is enforceable for a shipment of steel. It is nearly unenforceable for intangible assets.


Timing: 23–27 minutes. Define the two terms the syllabus names, and define them against each other.
Transfer pricing is the general practice of setting prices for transactions between commonly owned companies. It is unavoidable and mostly mundane. A German subsidiary buying finished goods from a Polish subsidiary has to record some price.
Profit shifting is the use of those prices, and of where entities are placed, to move taxable income from a higher-rate jurisdiction to a lower-rate one. The tool is the same; the purpose is different.
The arm’s-length principle is the international standard meant to keep the first from becoming the second. It works when a comparable transaction exists between unrelated parties. For a commodity or a standard component, a benchmark price is available. For rights to a design or a patent portfolio that exists nowhere else, there is no benchmark, and the price becomes an argument between a firm’s advisers and a revenue authority.
Duhigg and Kocieniewski make the general version of this point: profits that derive from royalties on intellectual property, or from products that are themselves digital, move far more easily than profits from physical goods. A downloaded application, unlike a car, can be sold from anywhere. That is why they find the 71 technology companies in the S&P 500 paying worldwide cash taxes at a rate roughly a third below other S&P companies.
Ask students to state the consequence: the more of a firm’s value sits in intangible assets, the more discretion it has over where profit appears.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The route the profit took
text:
The route the profit took


Apple was a pioneer of this structure, and the reporters find that hundreds of corporations later copied it.


Timing: 27–31 minutes. Take the diagram one arrow at a time and name what each step accomplished.
Apple created two Irish subsidiaries, today named Apple Operations International and Apple Sales International, and built a factory in Cork. The Irish government offered tax breaks in exchange for jobs. The larger advantage was that the arrangement let Apple send royalties on patents developed in California to Ireland, so those profits met the Irish rate of roughly 12.5 per cent rather than the US statutory rate of 35 per cent. By 2004, Ireland, with fewer than five million people, was home to more than a third of Apple’s worldwide revenues.
The second Irish company, the “double,” let other profits reach tax-free companies in the Caribbean. Apple assigned partial ownership of its Irish subsidiaries to Baldwin Holdings Unlimited in the British Virgin Islands, which had no listed office or telephone number and whose only listed director was Apple’s chief financial officer, working in Cupertino.
The Dutch step used Ireland’s treaties with European nations to let profits travel almost tax-free, and made them, in the reporters’ phrase, close to invisible to outside observers. A former Apple controller called the strategy the worst-kept secret in Europe.
Emphasise that this required no secrecy in the legal sense. It followed from ordinary rules that were each defensible alone and left a gap where they met. Say plainly that the structure has since been closed, and that the class will get to how and with what result.
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Selling in Germany on behalf of Singapore
text:
Selling in Germany on behalf of Singapore



From the 1980s Apple designated overseas distributors as commissionaires rather than retailers.

A commissionaire never technically takes possession of inventory, so it does not recognise the income.
A salesperson in high-tax Germany could sell on behalf of a low-tax subsidiary in Singapore.

Why it matters
The customer, the shop, and the salesperson do not move.
Only the identity of the legal seller changes, and with it the country that may tax the sale.


To the customer the change was invisible. To two treasuries it decided who collected.


Timing: 31–34 minutes. This mechanism is separate from the royalty route and students routinely miss it. The royalty route moves profit by pricing an intangible asset. The commissionaire structure moves profit by changing which company is legally the seller, without moving a single person or product.
Michael Rashkin, Apple’s first director of tax policy, helped set the system up before leaving in 1999, and the reporters describe Apple as among the first major corporations to use it.
Flag forward explicitly, because the payoff arrives later in the class. Hold on to Germany. When we reach the 2026 disclosure filings, Germany reappears with numbers attached, and students should be able to connect the mechanism described in 2012 to the pattern visible in the data fourteen years later.
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: A few dozen employees in Luxembourg
text:
A few dozen employees in Luxembourg



When customers across Europe, Africa, or the Middle East downloaded a song, show, or app, the sale was recorded at iTunes S.à r.l. in Luxembourg.

In 2011 that subsidiary’s revenue exceeded $1bn, roughly a fifth of iTunes’s worldwide sales, from a country of half a million people.

Why the digital case is sharper
A former Apple executive put it plainly: downloads are unlike tractors or steel because there is nothing you can touch.
If you buy from Luxembourg, it is a relationship with Luxembourg.


Levinson’s container still had to be unloaded somewhere. A download does not.


Timing: 34–37 minutes. This is the cleanest illustration of why the tax problem grew with the digital economy, and it links straight back to the container session.
Draw the contrast explicitly. A physical good arrives at a port, is declared, is valued, and is taxed by a state that can see it. The state’s capacity to tax rested partly on its ability to observe a physical event at a border it controlled. A digital sale has no such moment. The only thing fixing the sale to a place is a contractual decision about which company in the group is the seller.
The quoted executive is Robert Hatta, who oversaw iTunes retail marketing and sales for European markets until 2007. He is explicit that the reason for choosing Luxembourg was the favourable tax treatment. The reporters note that the country promised low rates to Apple and other technology firms in exchange for routing transactions through it, so taxes that would otherwise have gone to Britain, France, the United States, and dozens of other governments went to Luxembourg at a discount.
Ask what Luxembourg contributed to the transaction. The honest answer is a legal seat, a tax treatment, and a small staff. Then ask the harder question: is that different in kind from what Ireland contributed, or only in degree?
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: What the structure was worth
text:
What the structure was worth



3.2%


Apple’s tax rate on foreign profits in 2011, and 2.2% in 2010, in single digits for half a decade


About 70 per cent of profits were allocated overseas: $24bn of $34.2bn.
Worldwide, Apple paid $3.3bn cash tax on $34.2bn of profit, a rate of 9.8 per cent. Wal-Mart paid 24 per cent that year.

Sullivan estimated the US bill would have been about $2.4bn higher had profits been split evenly.



Timing: 37–41 minutes. Lead with the foreign rate rather than the blended one, because 3.2 per cent is the number that shows what the structure actually did. The 9.8 per cent worldwide figure blends in the more heavily taxed US profits and understates the effect.
The Wal-Mart comparison is the one to press: $5.9bn of cash taxes on $24.4bn of booked profit, which the reporters describe as about average for non-technology companies. Same country, same year, same corporate tax code, roughly two and a half times the rate. The difference is not the law but what the firm sells and where it can put the rights to it.
Handle the numbers honestly, because the article does. Cash taxes may cover multiple years, a company’s taxable income differs from the profits in its annual report, and Apple’s own disclosure listed worldwide taxes of $8.3bn, an effective rate near a quarter, a figure analysts regard as overstating what will ever be paid. Kimberly Clausing of Reed College is blunt that 10-K information is unreliable for most companies and worse for technology firms. Tell students that the measurement problem is itself a finding: the public cannot easily learn what a multinational pays, which is what makes the 2026 disclosure rule significant.
Martin Sullivan’s estimate is a counterfactual and should be labelled one. His reasoning is that since the marketing and product design are done in the United States and the patents were created in California, the US share should be at least 50 per cent rather than 30. Edward Kleinbard, former chief of staff of the Congressional Joint Committee on Taxation, adds the point that matters most for this course: the strategy does not only reduce US tax, but German, French, and British tax as well.
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: A mile and a half from Cupertino
text:
A mile and a half from Cupertino



De Anza College, where Steve Wozniak studied, cut more than a thousand courses and 8 per cent of its faculty after 2008. Its president described a budget “death spiral.”

California faced a shortfall above $9bn, having cut health programmes, raised university tuition, and proposed deep reductions in school spending.

The exchange at the City Council
Asked in 2011 whether Apple might provide free Wi-Fi to Cupertino, Steve Jobs answered that this is what taxes are for.
If the company could avoid paying them, he said, he would gladly put up Wi-Fi.


The college president was clear that he could not afford to press the point, because the school needs every dollar it can get.


Timing: 41–44 minutes. This section is why the article won a Pulitzer, and it is where the course’s distributional question enters. Do not moralise; let the facts do the work.
The causal claim must stay careful. Apple is not responsible for California’s budget crisis, which has many causes, and the article says so. Brian Murphy, De Anza’s president, treats the company’s tax position as symptomatic rather than causal. His stronger observation is about proximity: Apple employees’ children swim in the college’s pool and take classes there, and within twenty minutes of the campus sit the headquarters of Google, Facebook, Intel, Hewlett-Packard, and Cisco.
Add the part students find most surprising, which is that California legislated much of this itself. Increases to the state research and development credit in 1996, 1999, and 2000 let hundreds of companies avoid billions, with Apple reporting $412m of savings from credits of all kinds since 1996. In 2009, after lobbying led by Apple, Cisco, Oracle, and Intel, the legislature cut taxes for California-based corporations operating elsewhere, at an eventual cost analysts put near $1.5bn a year. The state was bidding for these firms at the same time as it was losing revenue from them.
Then the Jobs exchange, which is worth reading aloud from the record. Councilwoman Kris Wang asked how residents would benefit from the new headquarters and suggested free municipal Wi-Fi. Jobs replied that paying taxes is how the city gets those things, and offered the Wi-Fi only if Apple could stop paying them. He suggested the company could move if the Council were unhappy. Wang dropped the suggestion. Apple was Cupertino’s largest taxpayer, with more than $8m in property taxes assessed that year.
That is a bargaining exchange conducted in public, and it is a preview of Module 5. Ask who had leverage and what each side could credibly threaten.
[Source] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The firm’s defence, and the argument underneath it
text:
The firm’s defence, and the argument underneath it


What the company said
It complied with applicable laws and accounting rules, and is consistently among the world’s largest taxpayers.
In 2026 it added that corporate income tax is paid where assets are held, while VAT is paid where consumers are.
Executives argued privately that paying more would disadvantage them against rivals doing the same.

The deeper claim in the reporting
Tax codes were written for an industrial age and are ill suited to a digital economy.
Value now sits in royalties and downloads, which can be sold from anywhere.


If the rules produce this result, the interesting question is why no government has changed them.


Timing: 44–47 minutes. Give the company’s position its strongest form. Legality is not a technicality here. A firm that paid more than the law required would be making a discretionary transfer of shareholders’ money, and its competitors would not follow. Managers face something close to a collective action problem, and the structure becomes close to obligatory once rivals adopt it.
Apple’s 2012 statement said it had conducted its business to the highest ethical standards and that its US operations generated almost $5bn in federal and state income taxes in the first half of that fiscal year. The reporters note that the figure was unexplained, said nothing about deferred taxes, and appears to include income taxes owed by employees on stock gains. Use this as a lesson in reading a corporate statement: the number is probably accurate and answers a question nobody asked.
The 2026 distinction Apple draws in the FT is more sophisticated and deserves a hearing. Corporate income tax is levied where assets and risks sit; consumption taxes are levied where customers are; so a country whose consumers buy a great deal still collects substantially, just through a different tax. Ask students whether that is a satisfying answer to Kleinbard’s objection, and whether it would satisfy a German finance minister.
The second column is the analytical contribution. Twentieth-century rules allocate profit using physical presence, because in the economy that produced them, profit came from things that had locations. When the most valuable asset is a portfolio of rights, location stops constraining anything.
Close by setting up the second half. Governments knew about these structures for years, and Ireland was not a passive victim. Ask what Ireland was getting, and hold the answer until after the activity.
[Sources] - Duhigg and Kocieniewski, “How Apple Sidesteps Billions in Taxes.” - Jamie John, “Apple paid $17bn in taxes to Ireland after court ruling on back levies,” Financial Times, August 21, 2026.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Sort the moves
text:
Sort the moves

Classify each move: ordinary business choice · tax planning · abuse of the rules · illegal. Then name the government that lost revenue, if any.




Placing a subsidiary in Reno to hold investment income
Sending royalties on California patents to an Irish subsidiary
Letting a German salesperson sell on behalf of Singapore
Routing the royalty onward through the Netherlands



Booking every European app download in Luxembourg
Ireland granting tax breaks in exchange for jobs in Cork
California cutting taxes for firms operating out of state
Moving the intellectual property into Ireland when the route closed



Pick the one your group could not agree on. Was the difficulty the facts, the law, or your standard?


10 minutes · Groups of 3–4


Timing: 47–57 minutes. The categories are deliberately not parallel. Three are legal judgments and one is an ethical judgment, and groups should notice the mismatch rather than be told about it.
Take item 3 first when you debrief. Almost every group calls it tax planning at worst, and it moves an entire country’s sales income without moving a person, a product, or a customer. The gap between how the move feels and what it does is the point of the exercise.
Items 6 and 7 are the ones that carry the second half, because they are moves by governments rather than by the firm. Ireland traded tax treatment for employment in Cork; California cut taxes for companies operating elsewhere after those companies lobbied for it. Ask whether a state can be said to lose revenue it deliberately chose to forgo, and who inside each state actually decided.
Item 8 describes what happened after reform, and most groups will treat it as unremarkable. Return to that reaction when you reach Setser.
Do not supply a correct classification. The purpose is to establish that legal and acceptable are separate axes, and that the second is a political judgment which different governments were making differently.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Where would your industry book its profit?
text:
Where would your industry book its profit?

In your team’s industry, what is the most valuable thing the firm owns, and where could it be legally held?


A firm whose value sits in a patent, a brand, or a data set has options that a firm whose value sits in a mine or a rail line does not.


3 minutes · Industry teams


Timing: 57–60 minutes. Keep this short and take three or four answers across different industries. The comparison is the payoff, so call on teams whose industries sit at opposite ends.
Pharmaceuticals and software will find the question easy, because the patent or the code can be owned anywhere. Mining, shipping, utilities, and retail property will find it hard, because the asset is physically fixed and the state it sits in can tax it without the firm’s cooperation. That contrast is a source of leverage and dependence, which is what the industry project asks each team to locate.
Note the exception aloud for any team with a physically fixed asset. Those firms have less discretion over tax but far more exposure to the bargaining problem in Module 5, because an asset that cannot move can be taxed or seized after it is built.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Ireland was ordered to collect tax it did not want
text:
Ireland was ordered to collect tax it did not want


Ireland spent eight years and considerable public money resisting a judgment worth €13 billion to its own treasury.


Timing: 60–64 minutes. Establish the sequence before the legal reasoning, and let the strangeness of Ireland’s position sit for a moment.
The Commission’s instrument was state aid law rather than tax law, which matters. The European Union has very limited authority over member states’ direct taxation, and Ireland’s rate was never the target. What the Commission could reach was a selective advantage granted by a state to a particular firm, prohibited because it distorts competition within the single market. The case was framed as competition law and the remedy was recovery of the advantage rather than a fine.
Ask the class why Ireland fought a case it stood to win financially. The answer is the logic of the country’s development model. Ireland’s asset is the credibility of its commitment to firms that make long-lived investments on the strength of it. Conceding that its rulings were unlawful aid would put a price on that credibility well above €13 billion. Ireland was defending the arrangement, not resisting the money.
That is a bargaining position, and it prepares Module 5 directly.
[Sources] - European Commission decision on state aid to Apple, 2016. - Court of Justice of the European Union, Commission v. Ireland and Others, C-465/20 P, judgment of 10 September 2024.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The company that lived nowhere
text:
The company that lived nowhere


What the rulings allowed
Most of the profit of the Irish companies was attributed to a “head office.”
That head office had no premises, no employees, and no activity of its own.

What the Court held in 2024
The profits should have been allocated to the Irish branches that actually did the work.
Ireland had granted an advantage available to no one else, producing a rate below 1 per cent.


The structure collapsed on the question of whether an entity that does nothing can earn anything.


Timing: 64–67 minutes. This is the analytical centre of the second half, so slow down.
Distinguish it carefully from the 2012 diagram. In the structure Duhigg and Kocieniewski described, the profit’s destination was a real company in a real place that levied no tax, in the British Virgin Islands. What the Commission attacked was subtler: an internal allocation in which nearly all the profit of Apple Sales International and Apple Operations Europe belonged to head offices that existed only on paper and were tax resident nowhere at all. The first arrangement moves profit to a jurisdiction that chooses not to tax. The second moves it outside every jurisdiction’s reach.
The Court of Justice set aside the General Court’s 2020 judgment and confirmed the Commission’s approach. The correct comparison was between the Irish branches and the head offices, and since the head offices had no capacity to generate the profits, the profits belonged to the branches and were taxable in Ireland.
Draw out the general principle, because it is what students should carry beyond this case. The arm’s-length standard broke down when applied to an entity with no personnel and no functions, because there was nothing to price. What restored it was a substance test asking where the people who make the decisions actually are. That test now runs through international tax rules, and it explains why later reforms pushed firms to put real activity where they book profit rather than to stop booking it there.
Return to the board list from the opening. Ask which of the rules the class proposed the Court effectively applied.
[Source] - Court of Justice of the European Union, C-465/20 P, judgment of 10 September 2024, reinstating the Commission’s 2016 decision.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: What the ruling cost, and what disclosure revealed
text:
What the ruling cost, and what disclosure revealed



$17bn


income tax Apple paid to Ireland in the year to September 2025, out of $43bn paid worldwide


That is 40 per cent of its worldwide corporate income tax, in a country holding about 3 per cent of its workforce.
A quarter of Apple’s global pre-tax profit was booked through its Irish entities.

The figures are public because new EU rules require a country-by-country breakdown.



Timing: 67–70 minutes. Three separate points live here; keep them apart.
The first is magnitude. A single year’s payment to a country of about five million people made up around forty per cent of the firm’s worldwide corporate income tax. Most of that reflects the release of the escrowed back taxes rather than the ordinary annual liability, so it is a one-off in level while still being evidence about the scale of what had accumulated.
The second is the ratio that matters more than the total: a quarter of global pre-tax profit booked through entities in a country holding roughly three per cent of the workforce. That single comparison is the empirical version of the diagram from earlier in the class.
The third point is the most durable and the easiest to skip. The numbers are known because the European Union now requires large companies to break out revenues, profits, and corporate income taxes for every jurisdiction in the bloc and for designated tax havens. For the whole period covered by the 2012 article, no government and no journalist could see this jurisdiction by jurisdiction. The reporting obligation is what made the pattern visible, and it changed leverage without changing a single rate.
Note that this is spreading. Australia is expected to publish similar breakdowns, and new US accounting rules require listed companies to state whether and how overseas operations reduced their US tax bills.
[Source] - Jamie John, “Apple paid $17bn in taxes to Ireland after court ruling on back levies,” Financial Times, August 21, 2026.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The same firm, two European countries
text:
The same firm, two European countries


Ireland
5,575 employees
$6m of pre-tax profit per employee

Germany
4,089 employees
$51,000 of pre-tax profit per employee


Comparable headcounts, and a difference of more than a hundredfold in the profit each worker appears to generate.


Timing: 70–74 minutes. This is the single most useful slide in the session, because it converts an abstract argument into a measurement students can check.
Give them the arithmetic before the interpretation. The two countries have broadly similar Apple headcounts. If profit per employee measured anything about what workers do, the numbers would be within range of each other. They differ by a factor of well over a hundred. Ask what the ratio is actually measuring, and lead them to the answer: not productivity, but the location of the legal rights to which the profit attaches.
Germany is where the commissionaire structure from 2012 pointed, so close that loop explicitly. Apple paid $153m in cash taxes in Germany, about 0.3 per cent of its worldwide total. A mechanism the reporters described from executive interviews in 2012 is now visible as a line in a public filing.
Two further comparisons are worth putting on the board. Microsoft disclosed in June 2026 that it booked 38 per cent of global pre-tax profit in Ireland, more than $7m per employee. Procter & Gamble reported $115m of profit and no tax in Luxembourg, where it had one employee; the company said it had ceased operations there and had offset the profit with prior-year losses.
Give the objections a fair hearing, because they are not frivolous. Companies argue the rules paint an incomplete picture. The National Foreign Trade Council warns the figures can double-count revenue when subsidiaries sell to one another. Microsoft noted that a French entry reflecting a refund of overpaid tax shows how a single line can look strange without context. Ask students what additional information would let them distinguish an artefact of the rules from real profit shifting.
[Source] - John, “Apple paid $17bn in taxes to Ireland after court ruling on back levies.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Every reform ran through Ireland
text:
Every reform ran through Ireland


Setser’s argument: each attempt to tax these profits enlarged the system that books them in Ireland.


Timing: 74–78 minutes. Reconstruct both waves concretely, because the irony only lands if the mechanism is clear. Setser dates the run of luck from 2014, the year he describes Apple putting on a green jersey and becoming a tax resident of Ireland.
The first wave came out of the OECD’s base erosion work. Members agreed to end double Irish structures, so an Irish-registered subsidiary could no longer be a tax resident of Bermuda or the Caymans, and the Caribbean destination became untenable. Firms did not abandon the structure. They Irish-shored the intellectual property instead, which is Setser’s central point: getting rid of the double Irish was a boon to Ireland.
The mechanism is worth spelling out, because “moving the IP” sounds like paperwork and was in fact enormously valuable. Setser’s footnote describes Apple moving the rights to profit from sales outside the Americas to a Jersey subsidiary, which its main Irish subsidiary then notionally purchased. The notional interest financing that purchase was deductible against Irish income, and a capital allowance let Apple write off the notional cost over years, generating a deduction he puts at around €20 billion a year. Ireland acquired the tax base and simultaneously handed back much of the tax on it.
The second wave raised the minimum rate to 15 per cent, and Ireland collected more on the profits already sitting there. Two caveats matter. Setser notes a carveout for the United States, and he is explicit that most firms do not actually pay 15 per cent in Ireland, because capital allowances pull the effective rate down for firms like Apple and Microsoft.
Flag the apparent conflict between two of the readings, because a careful student will spot it. Setser says the reforms forced Ireland to raise its headline rate to 15 per cent; the FT says Ireland’s rate is 12.5 per cent at present. Both are right about different things. The 12.5 per cent headline still applies generally, while the 15 per cent minimum bites on the largest groups. Use this to make a point about reading sources: two reliable outlets can state different rates because “the rate” is not one number.
The US reforms did not remove the incentive either. Deferral was replaced in 2017 by a minimum rate near 10.5 per cent, which Setser argues encouraged pharmaceutical firms to keep offshore structures, and the 2025 legislation kept that basic pro-offshoring design while lifting the minimum to roughly 12.6 per cent.
Make sure students see why this is not a drafting failure. Both waves attacked the destination of profit rather than the mechanism that moves it, and both required firms to put substance where they book income. Ireland already had substance, an English-speaking workforce, EU market access, and a long record of accommodation. A rule requiring real activity in the jurisdiction of booking favours whichever compliant jurisdiction has the most real activity.
[Sources] - Brad W. Setser, “The Luck of the Irish,” Council on Foreign Relations, Follow the Money, March 16, 2026. - John, “Apple paid $17bn in taxes to Ireland after court ruling on back levies.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Ireland’s position is now a dependence
text:
Ireland’s position is now a dependence



≈€35bn


Irish corporation tax revenue in 2025, on close to €300bn of profit reported there by foreign multinationals


Setser puts a little under half of that down to three companies: Apple, Microsoft, and Eli Lilly. Their combined Irish payments come to over €16bn.
Microsoft books more than 80 per cent of its offshore profit in Ireland.

A state that depends on three firms for much of its tax revenue is in a bargaining relationship, not a regulatory one.



Timing: 78–81 minutes. Give the scale first and then the vulnerability.
Ireland has a population of about five million. Corporation tax has become one of the largest sources of revenue for the state, and the growth is concentrated in a small number of foreign-owned technology and pharmaceutical firms. The Irish Fiscal Advisory Council has warned that three firms account for almost half of receipts, and that this concentration is itself a risk.
Setser’s firm-level figures are worth having to hand. Apple is thought to have paid about €5.8bn in Irish tax in 2024 and Microsoft about €4.8bn, with Eli Lilly paying $6.6bn in 2025. Eli Lilly replaced Pfizer in the top three a couple of years ago, and Setser notes that its 2025 figure is inflated by a prepayment made ahead of tariffs that did not materialise, plus a prior-year payment.
Guard against one confusion that is easy to fall into. Setser’s “$17-18 billion” is the combined ordinary Irish tax of all three firms. The FT’s $17bn is Apple alone in the year to September 2025, inflated by the €13bn of recovered back taxes. The two numbers are close by coincidence and measure different things. If a student cites one for the other, that is a good moment to talk about reading figures carefully.
Then make the analytical turn, which is what the session is finally for. Ireland is usually described as the winner here, and in revenue terms it is. But the revenue rests on decisions those firms could reverse. If a US reform makes it attractive to bring the intellectual property home, or if one company restructures, Ireland loses a large share of its budget without any Irish policy having changed.
Ask who has leverage over whom. Ireland can set a rate. The firms decide where profit is booked, and that decision determines whether the rate applies to anything. Neither side can simply impose an outcome. This is the mutual dependence Module 5 studies with Apple and the Chinese state.
[Sources] - Setser, “The Luck of the Irish.” - Irish Fiscal Advisory Council, on the concentration of Irish corporation tax receipts.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: The revenue did not vanish. It changed government.
text:
The revenue did not vanish. It changed government.



Eli Lilly’s cash tax payments to Ireland in 2025 were twice its US federal tax payments, largely on profit generated by sales in the United States.

Setser’s judgement is that the United States should not keep a tax code that both allows and rewards moving its tax base offshore.

How he makes it vivid
He converts the forgone US revenue into warships: roughly four nuclear attack submarines a year from three firms.
The question to ask
Is that the right frame for what is, on his own account, a dispute between two friendly governments?


Every rule change so far has moved the base to another state. None has made it disappear.


Timing: 81–84 minutes. This is where the writing exercise finally gets its answer, so connect back to the board explicitly.
Lead with Eli Lilly, because it is the cleanest statement of the problem in any of the three readings. A US pharmaceutical company paid Ireland twice what it paid the US federal government, on profit that Setser says was largely generated by American sales. Ask the class which government has the better claim, and then point out that this is exactly the question they tried to answer with a rule at the start of class. Setser is not neutral: he treats these as US-source profits. A student could reasonably argue that the Irish operations are real, that manufacturing genuinely happens in Ireland, and that the claim is therefore weaker than he makes it sound. Let that argument be made.
He notes the pattern is not confined to one firm. Pfizer has large operations in Ireland and Singapore, Merck in Ireland and Switzerland, and AbbVie retains an Irish-Caribbean structure.
Handle the defence framing critically rather than just repeating it. Setser converts the lost revenue into aircraft carriers and submarines, and remarks that Ireland free rides on NATO while running a small defence budget despite the windfall. It is a memorable device and students will remember the submarines. Ask them what it does to the argument. It makes the sum feel concrete, and it also reframes a technical dispute over tax allocation as a question of national security and allied burden-sharing. That reframing is a political move, and it is worth naming as one even if you find the underlying point persuasive.
His closing line is that he raises a glass to Ireland for navigating global tax reform and emerging with more profits and more revenue than ever. The irony is the argument: reform kept redirecting the base rather than recapturing it.
[Source] - Setser, “The Luck of the Irish.”

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Three lessons about the legal border
text:
Three lessons about the legal border


The border is chosen
Distance and currency were imposed on the firm. Where profit is reported is decided by the firm, within rules states write.

Rules follow the old economy
Allocation rules were built for physical assets. Rights and downloads have no location the rules can hold onto.

Reform reassigns, it does not abolish
Every rule change moved the tax base to another state. None of them made it disappear.


Tax competition is states bidding for a base that firms can place. The bidding does not end when the rules tighten.


Timing: 84–86 minutes. Keep this to the three claims and resist adding a fourth.
On the first, the contrast with the two previous sessions is the reason this session sits in the module. The container changed a cost the firm faced. The baht changed a price the firm could not control. The jurisdiction of profit is a variable the firm sets, subject to constraints governments write and revise.
On the second, connect back to Read’s pencil and to the East India Company. Institutions built for one technology of production misfire when production changes, and the lag between the change and the institutional response is where firms earn returns. Profit shifting is a clean instance of a general claim in this course.
On the third, do not let students conclude reform is futile. The Court of Justice decision recovered €13 billion, the disclosure rules made the pattern visible, and the minimum rate raised the floor. What reform did not do was settle which state has the claim, because that is a distributive question between governments and no technical fix answers it.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Reflection: Return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: Return to your IB Voice

Would your rule have survived contact with the firms and the states in this session?


Revisit the rule you wrote at the start. Say what it would have done to the profit in this case, and name the government that would have fought it.


Timing: 86–89 minutes. Return students to their own claim and ask for one revision grounded in the session.
Strong revisions do one of two things. Some keep the rule and accept its distributive consequence explicitly, naming the loser and defending the loss. Others abandon a principle-based rule and argue the allocation is necessarily a negotiated outcome among states, in which case ask what determines each side’s bargaining power.
Do not require agreement. The measure of a good answer is whether the student has stopped treating “tax it where the value is created” as an answer and started treating it as a claim one government must enforce against another government’s claim.

title: One Firm, Many Legal Jurisdictions
section: Wednesday: how states write the rules together
text:
Wednesday: how states write the rules together

If states compete for the same tax base, why do they ever agree on common rules?


Irwin and Rivoli on trade agreements: the same problem of competing national claims, settled through negotiation rather than litigation.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. Set up the handoff precisely, because the two sessions are closer than they look.
Today ended with governments making rival claims on one tax base, resolved through a court and a multilateral minimum rate. Wednesday examines the older and larger institution built for the same problem in trade. Most-favoured-nation treatment, preferential agreements, and rules of origin are all devices for deciding which state’s rules apply to a transaction that touches several.
Ask students to come with one thought. The tax case was settled by a court applying competition law, while trade disputes are settled by agreements states negotiate and can leave. Which method binds a government more, and why might a state prefer the weaker one?

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Bernstein and Keay address different questions
text:
Bernstein and Keay address different questions


August 31 · Bernstein
How are trade rules created, contested, evaded, and changed?
Restricted access · illicit commerce · domestic conflict · coercion

September 2 · Keay
What kind of organization made this trade possible?
Risk · chartered monopoly · armed commerce · delegated authority


Today we study political conflict over trade. Wednesday we dive into corporate power.


Timing: 0–3 minutes. Explain the fixed reading sequence. Bernstein begins with the mature political economy of long-distance trade: restricted access, monopoly, illicit commerce, distributional conflict, coercion, and changing rules. Keay then steps back to explain the organizational form that made such trade possible and accumulated quasi-state powers. Do not resolve the EIC organizational puzzle today.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


Britain and China had traded at Canton for over a century without war. In 1839 they went to war. What changed? Defend your answer with evidence from the reading.



10 minutes · Individual · Notes allowed · No internet or LLMs


Timing: 3–13 minutes. Ask students to choose a primary explanation and defend it with chapter evidence. The purpose is to generate competing hypotheses before the lecture reconstructs the sequence. Do not resolve the question. Strongest answer is roughly: enforcement became urgent for Beijing at the same moment restraint disappeared on the British side, and the confiscation turned a smuggling dispute into a Crown liability.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Hypotheses
text:
Hypotheses

What explains the war?


Take each one: was it also true in 1780?


Timing: MM–MM minutes.
Take four or five answers and write each on the board as a short phrase. Do not sort or group them. Then advance to reveal the second question and work down the board one hypothesis at a time. Anything true in 1780 has a timing problem the student needs to solve; anything that is not is a candidate cause, so ask that student what set it off when it did. Leave the board list standing for the rest of class.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Canton permitted trade on Qing terms
text:
Canton permitted trade on Qing terms





The Qing state confined Western foreign trade to Canton and licensed Chinese hongs (merchant houses).

The aim was to keep silver at home and foreign influence out.

Qing authorities used the Canton system to control the terms of foreign trade.



William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 18–22 minutes. Define the Canton System through three controls: where foreigners could trade, through whom, and under what conditions. Explain that concern about silver outflows is recognizably mercantilist, while the broader objective is sovereignty: obtain gains from trade while limiting foreign penetration, dependence, and political influence.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - William Daniell, View of the Canton Factories, 1805–06, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Britain paid for tea with silver
text:
Britain paid for tea with silver



≈90%


of the value Britain sent to China was bullion


In 1751, Britain sent £119,000 in silver and £10,842 in merchandise.
Britain bought tea and silk. China bought little that Britain made.


The imbalance created pressure to find something China would buy.


Timing: 22–25 minutes. Bernstein reports that roughly 90 percent of the value of eighteenth-century British exports to China was bullion and provides the 1751 example. Ask whether the imbalance itself necessarily causes conflict or becomes dangerous through the responses it induces.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 286–287.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
text:
Mercantilism linked commerce to national power
State power: Commerce should strengthen the state
Bullion: Gold and silver supported public credit, military spending, and political power
Trade balance: Export surpluses brought bullion into the country
Empire: Colonies and chartered companies like EIC secured supplies, markets, shipping

Britain bought Chinese goods with silver while China bought little British merchandise. Mercantilists saw the outflow as a loss of national wealth and power.


Timing: 18–21 minutes. Define mercantilism as a view of commerce shaped by national power and rivalry. Bullion mattered because it supported public credit, military spending, and the fiscal capacity of the state. Mercantilists did not oppose all imports. Imports that strengthened national production or power could be valuable. Their concerns were dependency, bullion loss, and whether trade strengthened another state more than their own. Use this framework to explain why Britain’s persistent silver outflow to China appeared to require a solution.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, pp. 284–287. - Lars Magnusson, The Political Economy of Mercantilism (Routledge, 2015). - Francis Swaine, An East Indiaman in Stays, c. 1780, Royal Museums Greenwich / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: From cotton to opium
text:
From cotton to opium





The EIC grew and auctioned opium in India. Private traders carried it into China.


The increased imports led to silver outflows from China, which they tried to halt



Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 25–30 minutes. Explain the triangle briefly before the opium step: the EIC’s position in Bengal gave it Indian cotton, which China bought, so Britain routed trade through India to cover its bilateral imbalance with China; when Chinese demand for Indian cotton weakened, the commercial search continued and opium took cotton’s place. Then distinguish the Company’s legal position in India from the private traders’ illicit entry into China. The analytical point is strategic response: commercial and political actors chose an organizational solution to the imbalance.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–290. - Opium factory at Patna, c. 1851, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion
text:
Barriers created rents and rewarded evasion


Regulation redirected commerce through smugglers and intermediaries.


Timing: 30–33 minutes. Define rents as returns created by restricted access or an artificial price wedge. Chinese controls did not remove demand for market access; they encouraged organizational separation, intermediaries, smuggling, and illicit commerce. Save contemporary analogies for the end.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Production and finance kept the EIC at the center
text:
Production and finance kept the EIC at the center




The Company auctioned opium in India.
Private traders sold it in China for silver.
The silver bought Company bills.
EIC silver bought tea.

Infrastructural power: the EIC never carried opium into China, yet every stage of the trade ran through it.



The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839 · MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 33–37 minutes. Walk through the four steps of the circuit on the slide. Then ask the question the slide implies: how did the EIC shape an illegal trade that private merchants conducted? Introduce “infrastructural power”: the capacity to shape production, finance, and exchange without directing every transaction. Pose the organizational puzzle but do not solve it. Keay explains the origins of this capacity on September 2.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 287–291. - MIT Visualizing Cultures, The Opium Trade in China, 1833–1839.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis
text:
Lin Zexu turned tension into crisis



40,000


chests of opium a year by the late 1830s, four times the 1825 level



In 1839, Commissioner Lin detained foreign merchants and destroyed more than 20,000 chests of opium.

To the Qing court, this was enforcement of Chinese law and sovereignty.
To British merchants, it was an attack on property and commerce.


Timing: 37–42 minutes. Start with the numbers: the EIC lost its China monopoly in 1834, private firms such as Jardine Matheson combined the country trade with the tea trade, and Bernstein reports growth from roughly 10,000 to 40,000 chests. Removing one monopoly did not make the trading system lawful or apolitical. Lin’s intervention followed arrests of local smugglers and mounting social and fiscal consequences. Ask students to give the strongest account of each interpretation. The enforcement shock is endogenous: it arose from consequences produced by the trading regime itself.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 290–297.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Commercial interests mobilized military power
text:
Commercial interests mobilized military power





Merchants lobbied London for compensation and wider access. The government sent warships.


Britain’s use of military force to expand market access led to interstate conflict: the Opium War.



E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843 · National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures


Timing: 42–45 minutes. Jardine and other merchants pressed the British cabinet for a favorable treaty backed by naval force. The Nemesis was built for the EIC and designed for shallow Chinese waters. Emphasize the political translation from commercial grievance to state coercion.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 297–302. - E. Duncan, The Nemesis Destroying Chinese War Junks, 1843, National Maritime Museum / MIT Visualizing Cultures.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade
text:
The Treaty of Nanking rewrote the rules of trade


Indemnity · Hong Kong · five treaty ports · end of the hong monopoly · (eventually) low tariffs


John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846 · Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 45–48 minutes. No provision legalized opium. The treaty nevertheless changed market access, tariff authority, and territorial control; subsequent agreements expanded British privileges. Return briefly to the opening hypotheses: the imbalance was a pressure, restrictions shaped the response, commercial interests mobilized, and coercive state power changed the rules.
[Sources] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 302–304. - John Platt and John Burnet, The Signing of the Treaty of Nanking, 1846, Anne S. K. Brown Military Collection / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The Long Path to More Open Trade
text:
The Long Path to More Open Trade


Sovereignty → trade restrictions → rents → circumvention


Crackdown → interstate conflict → forced rule change


Responses to the trade imbalance transformed commercial tensions into interstate conflict.


Timing: 48–51 minutes. Abstract the mechanism only after reconstructing the case. This is one pathway: controlled access generates circumvention; growing consequences provoke enforcement; enforcement triggers interstate conflict; power then produces forced rule change.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: What did the Corn Laws actually do?
text:
What did the Corn Laws actually do?





Who is protected when wheat prices fall below 63 shillings? Who pays?



Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1


Timing: 51–54 minutes. Ask students to read the schedule before explaining it. When the domestic wheat price fell below 63 shillings, the 24.25-shilling import levy made foreign grain much more expensive. The rule protected domestic landowners and grain prices while raising food costs for consumers. Use their answers to introduce the distributional positions on the next slide.
[Source] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11, Table 11-1.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Free-trade ideas became a political program
text:
Free-trade ideas became a political program

Smith and Ricardo showed that protection raised costs and blocked gains from trade. Cobden’s League organized that argument into a campaign for repeal.

The League turned an abstract economic argument into policy.


Timing: 54–58 minutes. Comparative advantage appears here as part of the ideas component. Smith and Ricardo supplied a framework. Cobden and the Anti-Corn Law League converted it into a campaign. Landowner interests and parliamentary influence kept repeal blocked until 1845.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing
text:
Prepare a 30-second statement for the public hearing


5 minutes · Individual · Notes permitted


Maintain, modify, or repeal? Consider your two strongest arguments, who gains and who loses, and the strongest argument against your position.


Timing: 58–65 minutes. Physically divide the room into three sides. Assign students rather than allowing self-selection if one side is sparse. They are not formal groups: every student prepares an individual argument and may be called on. Establish the material stakes as you assign sides: landowners held concentrated interests and disproportionate institutional influence, industrialists were a rising economic constituency, and urban workers and consumers bore higher food costs without equivalent political power. Then circulate and press students to distinguish material interests, public arguments, and political leverage. Do not mention the famine.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 305–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Public hearing
text:
Public hearing

Should Britain maintain, modify, or repeal the Corn Laws?


We will hear from each side. Listen for interests, expected winners and losers, political influence, and ideas.


Timing: 65–74 minutes. Cold-call multiple students from each side for short testimony and rebuttal. On the board, sort claims under material interests, winners and losers, political influence, and arguments or ideas. Surface the stable protectionist equilibrium without yet naming shocks as the lesson.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Round 2
text:
Round 2

Does the shock change your position?

If yes, what changed in your reasoning? If no, how do you defend the existing policy now?

2 minutes · Individual reconsideration


Timing: 75–80 minutes. Give students two minutes, then take brief testimony from each side. Ask whether the shock changed material interests, moral and political costs, expectations about governing survival, or the viability of the existing coalition.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The famine raised the political cost of protection
text:
The famine raised the political cost of protection

Landowners gained from protection and dominated Parliament. But repeal was a known possibility already circulating in political debate.

The crisis fractured the governing coalition and made repeal possible.


Timing: 80–83 minutes. Interests and institutions remained in place. The shock raised the political cost of protection, strengthened an available policy alternative, and enabled political realignment under Peel.
[Source] - Bernstein, Chapter 11, pp. 310–312.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: Two pathways made trade rules unstable
text:
Two pathways made trade rules unstable


China
Restrictions
→ circumvention
→ crackdown
→ interstate conflict
→ forced rule change

Corn Laws
Distributional conflict
→ durable coalition
→ external shock
→ political realignment
→ liberalization


Rules create rents, coalitions defend them, institutions sustain them, and ideas plus shocks change them.


Timing: 83–87 minutes. Do not force the cases into one identical model. China’s enforcement shock emerged from the consequences of the trade regime and led to coercive interstate change. The famine was an external shock that changed domestic coalition politics. Then read the key line as the conceptual payoff: interests supply preferences; institutions weight those preferences; ideas supply interpretations and alternatives; shocks change the political costs and coalition possibilities. Ask students to name the actor, institution, idea, and destabilizing event in each case. Neither markets nor policy changes are self-executing, and repeal was political change, not the automatic implementation of economic truth.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The same mechanisms shape international business today
text:
The same mechanisms shape international business today







18th and 19th Centuries
International business today




Mercantilism and controlled access
Economic security and strategic sovereignty


Smuggling and intermediaries
Transshipment and sanctions evasion


EIC production and financial infrastructure
Big Tech dominance


Corn Law coalition and famine
Sectoral lobbying and crisis-driven realignment




When states constrain globalization, firms reorganize trade around the new limits.


Timing: 87–89 minutes. Keep the analogies brief. The claim is not that history repeats or that the cases are equivalent. The recurring mechanisms are controlled access, rents, circumvention, infrastructural power, distributional coalitions, and shock-driven realignment.

title: Who Sets the Rules of Trade?
section: The EIC puzzle remains
text:
The EIC puzzle remains

What kind of company could organize trade, finance, coercion, and political authority across continents?


On Wednesday we ask why long-distance trade required a chartered company and how that company acquired such immense power.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. Return to the unresolved EIC puzzle. Monday established the Company’s infrastructural capacity. Keay explains how long-distance risk and organizational problems produced the chartered-company form, and how capabilities created for commerce became foundations of political power and empire.

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: Ideas and skills that are uniquely your own
text:
Ideas and skills that are uniquely your own





Goldstein, describing a student


“If she wanted to be valuable on the job market, she felt, she would need to have ideas and skills that were uniquely her own.”


MIT report


“the most important product of their education is not a GPA or a diploma but themselves … the development of their own imagination, insight, and judgment.”



Writing first gives you a perspective of your own to test, defend, and revise.


Explain that this course does not reject AI. It distinguishes between using AI and allowing AI to substitute for the development of students’ own judgment.
[Sources] - Dana Goldstein, “What Do Students Lose When They Stop Writing?,” The New York Times, August 17, 2026 (assigned PDF on Canvas). - MIT, “AI and Education,” 2026, https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/report/ - Course asset assets/mit.png, provided by the instructor.

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: Your IB Voice
text:
Your IB Voice


Question


How is a Nespresso capsule possible? Explain what must be coordinated for this product to reach a consumer.



12 minutes · Individual · Blue book · Ungraded


I will collect your response and return it for you to critique during the final exam.


Place a Nespresso capsule or package where students can see it. Give students the preprinted response sheet and collect it immediately after 12 minutes, before discussion. The response is ungraded; the final-exam critique will be graded.

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: No one knows how to make the whole pencil?
text:
No one knows how to make the whole pencil?



No participant possesses all the knowledge required to make it. The logger, miner, chemist, machinist, and executive each know only part(s) of the process.


Why do they participate?
If no one directs the entire system, how does a pencil get made?

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: A powerful (yet incomplete) story
text:
A powerful (yet incomplete) story


What Read covers

Dispersed knowledge
Specialization and exchange
Markets and invisible hands
Coordination without a central planner


What Read does not cover

Firms, locations, and contracts
Standards, finance, and infrastructure
Governments, policies, and borders
Dependence, power, and disruption



Separate Read’s descriptive insight from his normative conclusion. Use the final question to pivot from market coordination to the firm as an organization and the state as rule-maker and political actor.
[Sources] - Leonard E. Read, “I, Pencil” (1958), https://fee.org/articles/i-pencil/

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: Reconstruct the system
text:
Reconstruct the system

What must happen before a Nespresso capsule reaches a consumer?


10 mins. Working in small groups, identify the actors, activities, inputs, places, and relationships you think are necessary.


Focus on what you can infer without additional research. Note what you would need more time to investigate.


Give groups approximately five minutes, then build one live diagram on the board. Do not provide categories at the start. As the diagram develops, probe what is coordinated by markets, by Nestlé hierarchy, by contracts, and by public rules.

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: Production inputs and supply chains
text:
Production inputs and supply chains





Coffee supply: farms, mills, and exporters
Capsule supply: aluminum body and seal, coating, and filters
Package supply: boxing, printing and adhesives
Factory: machinery, energy, and quality control
Production: roast, blend, grind, fill, seal, and pack
Distribution: cases, pallets, transport, customs, warehousing, and delivery



Show this only after the class has produced its own diagram. Ask which component supply chains and production inputs their reconstruction missed. Then ask what coordinates the actors before, within, and beyond the factory.
[Sources] - User-provided image, “What Nespresso Pods Are Actually Made Of: Layer by Layer”; original source not identified. - Nespresso, “Coffee Expertise,” https://www.nespresso.com/expertise/UK_en

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: One product contains three different problems
text:
One product contains three different problems


Market
How do prices incentivize specialized producers who do not know one another to coordinate?

Firm
What should Nestlé own, contract for (outsource), and locate in which countries?

State
What will governments and societies permit, require, or prevent? What causes the rules to change?


International business involves the interaction of all three.


Use this to introduce the firm as the course’s central unit of analysis without losing the market and political environment. Invite one example from the class diagram for each column.

title: How Is a Nespresso Capsule Possible?
section: Knowledge requires open exchange
text:
Knowledge requires open exchange



Yale Committee on Trust in Higher Education


Free speech as a first principle. “Colleges and universities have a special obligation to protect the classroom as a distinct place, where open exchange and structured conversation can thrive.”


MIT report
