title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: How did a nutmeg island become an imperial target?
text:
How did a nutmeg island become an imperial target?





Run was two miles long, had no fresh water, and produced nutmeg.

Its villages answered to no sultan. Councils of orang kaya governed each island as a self-governing republic.


Pulo Run had sovereignty of its own to give away.


Nutmeg tree (Myristica fragrans) © uforest.org


Timing: 17–20 minutes. Keay opens with Run because it makes the transition from trade to empire visible. The tree is Myristica fragrans. Keay describes it as “dark of foliage, willow-size, and carefully tended,” and notes it grew nowhere else on earth, which is the whole source of the rent. Establish the governance point now rather than later: thanks to their isolation the Banda islands “owed allegiance to no one,” authority rested with village councils under orang kaya, and in the tradition of adat each island was “a self-governing and fairly democratic republic.” They could “withhold or dispose of their sovereignty as they saw fit.” That is precisely why what happens in 1616 creates a legal problem the Company cannot absorb. Hold the 1616 pledge until the end of class.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i. - Map of the Banda Islands, Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The prize was extraordinary
text:
The prize was extraordinary





<½ penny → £1.60


Ten pounds of nutmeg
Banda purchase price → European sale price



One-sixth of a ship’s cargo could pay for the entire voyage.


Nutmeg fruit with mace


Timing: 24–26 minutes. Use the photograph. Both commodities are visible in one fruit: the dark seed is the nutmeg, and the lacy scarlet membrane around it is the mace. Mace cost roughly ten times more per pound at both ends because one tree yields far less of it.
Lead with the prices rather than a percentage. Keay states a figure of roughly 32,000 per cent, but his own prices imply a larger multiple still. Nutmeg and mace produce the same ratio, so the percentage is best left off the slide.
The sixth-of-a-cargo line is the one students should retain. It explains the business logic behind the mortality figures introduced later: extreme risk was tolerable because expected returns were enormous.
[Source] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–§ii.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Three forms of trade and sovereign power
text:
Three forms of trade and sovereign power


Portugal
A Crown enterprise
Capital: Crown and merchant contractors
Returns: Spice markups, customs, and licence fees to the Crown
Authority: Royal fleets, forts, and governors

The Dutch (VOC)
A sovereign company
Capital: Private shareholders
Returns: Dividends to investors; taxes and charter fees to the Dutch Republic
Authority: The VOC could make treaties, build forts, wage war, and govern territory

The English (EIC)
A more limited company
Capital: Private voyage subscribers
Returns: Profits to investors
Authority: Monopoly, factories, diplomacy, and armed ships, but no initial right to rule territory


All three fused commerce and state power. They differed in who paid, who profited, and who ruled.


Timing: 22–28 minutes. This slide does two jobs. Read the top half across as a comparison of institutional forms, then the bottom half across as the sequence that produced the English charter.
On the forms: do not imply all three were mature in 1600. Portugal’s system was long established, the English Company was chartered in December 1600, and the VOC in 1602.
Portugal ran a crown-administered maritime empire. Governors, fortified ports, and fleets controlled the strategic routes, and passing ships had to buy a licence from the Portuguese to trade — a system for taxing other people’s commerce without governing the territory it crossed. The claim rested on a papal grant that had divided the non-European world between Portugal and Spain, which is why the English regarded it as an “insolency” rather than a right. Papal authority linked Portugal’s commercial monopoly to conquest and the spread of Christianity. The papal bulls authorized conquest and colonization as well as trade and Christian evangelization.
The Dutch East India Company received extensive public powers from the Dutch Republic and combined commercial monopoly with treaties, armed conquest, and territorial rule, most brutally in the Banda Islands.
The English Company began with factories, diplomatic privileges, and armed shipping. Territorial and revenue-collecting government came much later, most consequentially in Bengal after 1765.
On the sequence: Keay is clear that Dutch success, not English ambition, was decisive. Lancaster’s 1591 reconnaissance had shown danger rather than profit. Dutch voyages in the late 1590s showed direct trade could pay, which doomed the Levant Company’s overland business. The final straw was news that the Dutch were buying English shipping, which let the petitioners argue that the national interest was at stake.
Note who the petitioners were: Muscovy and Levant Company men, “organized into powerful and exclusive syndicates with access to capital and influence, yet independent of both court and government.” That independence is about to come under pressure.
Asian rulers and merchants remained strategic actors throughout. The English entered an existing political economy rather than an open market.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–iv. - Sanjay Subrahmanyam, The Portuguese Empire in Asia, 1500–1700, 2nd ed. (Wiley-Blackwell, 2012). - Femme S. Gaastra, The Dutch East India Company (Walburg Pers, 2003).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Imperialism is broader than colonialism
text:
Imperialism is broader than colonialism


Imperialism
Extends effective control across territories and peoples.
It can operate through treaties, finance, monopoly, military force, or delegated company authority.
A local government may formally remain in place.

Colonialism
Places territory and people under sustained external rule.
Governing authority exercised by crown officials, settlers, or a chartered company.


An empire can dominate without establishing formal colonial rule. Colonialism entails assuming governance authority.


Timing: 20–22 minutes. Imperialism is the broader concept. It describes effective control exercised beyond a polity’s borders. That control can operate formally or informally through treaties, finance, commercial monopoly, military pressure, or authority delegated to a company. Local institutions may survive while their autonomy is sharply constrained.
Colonialism is a particular institutional form of imperialism. An external power assumes sustained authority over territory and people. Administration may be carried out by metropolitan officials, settlers, or a chartered company.
The distinction matters for Keay. Armed ships, exclusive trading rights, coercive seizures, and political treaties created imperial power before the East India Company governed a large colonial territory. Bantam remained a trading agency under a local ruler. Run raised a claim to territorial rule.
[Sources] - Michael W. Doyle, Empires (Cornell University Press, 1986), pp. 19, 30–47. - John Gallagher and Ronald Robinson, “The Imperialism of Free Trade,” Economic History Review 6, no. 1 (1953): 1–15. - Jürgen Osterhammel, Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Markus Wiener, 1997), pp. 15–20. - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Around 1600, European trade was one layer of a larger Asian network
text:
Around 1600, European trade was one layer of a larger Asian network

European trade was one small part of a much larger Asian network.


Timing: 26–28 minutes. Let the map carry the argument. Trace the dense, overlapping routes linking East Africa, Aden and the Red Sea, Hormuz and the Persian Gulf, Indian textile ports, Malacca, the Indonesian spice islands, and China.
Keay’s narrative begins at the European edge of this system, but the system itself was predominantly Asian. Chinese, Malay, Indian, Arab, Persian, and other merchants had long connected regional production and consumption. Around 1600, the English were a small new entrant into these established circuits, not the network’s organizing center.
Avoid implying that European participation was inconsequential. Portuguese, Dutch, and English armed shipping increasingly changed access, prices, and political bargains. The chronological point is that this intervention entered and then reshaped a much older commercial world.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii. - Om Prakash, European Commercial Enterprise in Pre-Colonial India (Cambridge University Press, 1998), Chapters 1–5. - Simeon Netchev, “Map of the Trade in the Indian Ocean 15th–16th century,” World History Encyclopedia, 2025, CC BY-NC-ND: https://www.worldhistory.org/image/20178/map-of-the-trade-in-the-indian-ocean-15th-16th-cen/

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Frontier shipping became a question of national power
text:
Frontier shipping became a question of national power




Lancaster’s Red Dragon: 600 tons · 38 guns · built for privateering · about 200 men


Isaac Sailmaker, Two Views of an East Indiaman, c. 1685 · National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


A frontier capability
Ocean-going hulls combined cargo capacity, firepower, trained crews, and navigational knowledge.
The trigger
Dutch merchants then tried to buy English ships.
The political claim
The petitioners told Elizabeth that the “national interest” was at stake.


The Crown needed a way to harness privately assembled strategic capacity.


Timing: 31–34 minutes. The delay in granting the charter is not the teaching point. The important development is that English merchants and privateers had assembled a viable long-distance shipping capability that the Crown could neither ignore nor leave entirely to private or foreign control.
Treat frontier technology as a system, not simply a hull. Direct Asian trade depended on naval architecture, artillery, large pools of capital, trained mariners, navigational knowledge, provisioning, and command experience. Lancaster’s Red Dragon illustrates the platform: about 600 tons, 38 guns, built for privateering, and able to carry roughly 200 men. The painting is a later seventeenth-century East Indiaman rather than Lancaster’s actual ship, but it shows the armed merchant-ship form.
Keay identifies the trigger. Dutch voyages demonstrated that direct trade with Asia could be profitable. When Dutch merchants sought to add English shipping to their fleets, the English petitioners argued that the “national interest” was at stake and carried their petition to Queen Elizabeth. A privately created commercial capability had become strategically important to the state.
End with the transition: the next slide explains the royal charter as the instrument used to incorporate, privilege, constrain, and harness that capacity.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii–iv. - Isaac Sailmaker, Two Views of an East Indiaman of the Time of King William III, c. 1685, National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The charter bestowed power
text:
The charter bestowed power
A royal charter was a sovereign grant creating a corporation and conferring legal privileges.


What it granted
Corporate status: continuity and internal governance
Monopoly: exclusive English trade beyond the Cape for 15 years
Enforcement: Company licenses; unlicensed trade risked forfeiture

Who gained
Subscribers: English rivals excluded; capital and voyage risk pooled
The Crown: privately financed maritime expansion; control over English participation


Merchants received monopoly returns while the Crown gained maritime authority.

section: Where does commercial coordination become imperial power?
text:
Where does commercial coordination become imperial power?

Explain the significance of each episode and classify it: commercial coordination · imperial power · colonial rule. More than one category may apply.

The 1600 royal charter
Lancaster’s dealings with Sultan Ala-uddin at Aceh
The seizure of a Portuguese carrack



The Bantam factory
Country-trade voyages
Run and Ai pledge allegiance to the English Crown through Company agents

Pick one episode your group could not agree on. What business problem did it solve? What authority did it exercise? Whose freedom of action did it limit?

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The risk undertaken because the returns were large
text:
The risk undertaken because the returns were large





25 of 198


men who rounded the Cape on Lancaster’s 1591 voyage reached England again

On the first Company fleet, 105 of 480 men were dead before it reached the Cape.


Investors accepted these odds because one-sixth of a cargo still returned a profit.


Portrait of Sir James Lancaster · National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 56–59 minutes. Two out of three ships were lost on Lancaster’s 1591 voyage. The only cargo to reach home was a boatload of scurvy victims. Keay writes that the experience should have discredited the project, but Dutch success revived investor interest.
On the first Company fleet, Lancaster prescribed three spoonfuls of lemon juice each morning aboard the Red Dragon. Its crew remained healthy through the scurvy latitudes while 105 men died before the Cape across the rest of the fleet. The remedy demonstrates a management problem: knowledge created value only when the organization adopted it beyond the individual commander.
Use the portrait to introduce Lancaster as a bundle of experience, reputation, and authority. His skills helped the Company operate, while dependence on one commander made the capability fragile.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iii–§iv. - Portrait of Sir James Lancaster, National Maritime Museum / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: At Aceh, Lancaster negotiated market access
text:
At Aceh, Lancaster negotiated market access




What Ala-uddin granted
A trading house, royal protection, full trading rights, and exemption from customs duties
What Elizabeth’s letter argued
No nation is self-sufficient, so distant countries should trade with one another.
Any prince who trades with only one European nation should expect political subordination to it.


England argued for open trade abroad while chartering a monopoly at home.


Theodor de Bry, Dutch envoys at Sultan Ala-uddin’s court, engraving published 1604 · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 59–62 minutes. The engraving shows Dutch visitors at Ala-uddin’s court, not Lancaster’s audience. It was published in 1604 and depicts the same Sultan and court at the time of Lancaster’s 1602 visit. Make that distinction explicit.
Lancaster used court ritual, gifts, translation, and Elizabeth’s letter to secure a trading house, royal protection, trading privileges, and exemption from customs duties. He prostrated himself “after the manner of the country.”
Spend time on what the letter actually argued, because it is the sharpest irony in the chapter. In His “infinite and unsearchable wisdom” God had arranged that no nation be self-sufficient, so that “out of the abundance of ffruit which some region[s] enjoyeth, the necessitie or wante of others should be supplied.” Distant countries should therefore have “traffique” with one another and become friends through “their interchange of commodities.” The letter then turns pointed: Spain and Portugal insist on exclusive trading rights, and any prince who grants them “must expect a degree of political subordination to that nation.”
England was making the case for open trade as a challenger, two years after chartering a monopoly of its own, and was warning Asian rulers against precisely the exclusive arrangement the Company existed to build. Ask students to hold both facts at once rather than resolve them. The argument was also genuinely useful to Ala-uddin, whose rivalry with Portuguese Malacca made open trade his interest too, which is why Keay says the sentiments “could have been his own.” The letters were sent unaddressed, with the recipient’s name filled in by whoever delivered them, so the same doctrine was offered to every ruler the English met.
Connect forward: the free-trade argument reappears on Monday’s side of the course as the case against the Corn Laws, made by manufacturers who benefited from it. Arguments for open trade tend to be advanced by whoever is currently excluded.
Aceh had killed an objectionable Dutch commander two years earlier and had repeatedly challenged Portuguese Malacca. Ala-uddin was selecting among European partners rather than submitting to one.
The commercial result was limited because the expected pepper had not arrived. Keay describes Aceh’s importance as political and strategic rather than commercial.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §ii and §iv, including the text of Elizabeth’s standard letter. - Theodor de Bry, Dutch visit to Sultan Ala-uddin’s court, engraving published 1604, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Armed seizure solved England’s export problem
text:
Armed seizure solved England’s export problem




What Lancaster sailed with
£20,000 in Spanish silver
£6,000 in English goods
What he took by force
Indian textiles that more than doubled his trading stock


England had little to sell, so silver and seizure supplied what the market would take.


Portuguese India Armada of 1502, from the Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu, c. 1565 · Morgan Library / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 64–67 minutes. The image depicts the Portuguese India Armada rather than Lancaster’s specific prize. Use it to establish the armed commercial system Lancaster entered.
Coercion was part of Lancaster’s strategy. On the 1591 reconnaissance voyage, Keay writes that no attempt was made to open honest trade. The targets included Asian and Portuguese shipping.
In 1602, Lancaster seized a Portuguese carrack carrying so many Indian calicoes that unloading took six days. Sultan Ala-uddin assisted by detaining a Portuguese emissary who might have raised the alarm. The captured textiles more than doubled Lancaster’s trading stock.
The cargo composition is the IB point. England made little that Southeast Asian merchants wanted. Lancaster carried bullion, then acquired Indian textiles that could purchase pepper and spices. Keay describes exploiting Asia’s existing carrying trade as an imperative.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iii–§iv. - Portuguese India Armada of 1502, Livro de Lisuarte de Abreu, c. 1565, Morgan Library / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Bantam was an early analogue of foreign direct investment
text:
Bantam was an early analogue of foreign direct investment




Without a factory
Each fleet arrival pushed spice prices up, pushed the price of its own cloth down, and left ships idle waiting for a return cargo.
With a factory
Resident factors bought and sold all year, so prices moved less and cargo was waiting when the fleet arrived.


Local presence changed the terms of every transaction the Company made.


View of Bantam, Java, early seventeenth century · Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 67–70 minutes. Separate the two mechanisms.
First, price effects. When a fleet arrived, it suddenly increased demand for spices and increased the local supply of imported cloth. Spice prices rose while prices for the Company’s cloth fell. Year-round factors could spread purchases and sales over time rather than transact at the fleet’s moment of maximum disadvantage.
Second, turnaround. Factors gathered information and assembled return cargo before the large ocean-going ships reached Bantam. The ships therefore spent less expensive time waiting in port.
Bantam is an early analogue of foreign direct investment because the Company replaced repeated export-market visits with a controlled, lasting commercial establishment abroad. Do not collapse the analogy into identity. The factory was a trading establishment rather than a modern incorporated affiliate or productive plant. It operated under a local ruler’s sovereignty and was not itself a colony.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §iv. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976). - View of Bantam, Java, Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The Company depended on an existing Asian regional network
text:
The Company depended on an existing Asian regional network





Aceh: diplomacy and political access
Priaman: pepper
Bantam: factory and regional hub
Banda: nutmeg and mace
Moluccas: cloves and subsidiary voyages



The Bantam factory connected large Company ships to smaller Asian vessels carrying goods and market intelligence.


Locator map prepared for this course · Coastlines from the R maps package (CIA World Data Bank II) · Banda inset schematic, positions accurate


Timing: 70–73 minutes. Orient students on the map before making the argument. Aceh sits at the northern tip of Sumatra and Priaman farther down its west coast. Malacca lies across the straits on the Malay peninsula, which is why control of that channel mattered so much to the Portuguese. Bantam lies at the western end of Java on the Sunda Strait. The Banda Islands and the Moluccas lie far to the east.
The distances are the point students miss. Bantam to Banda is roughly 1,500 miles, covered in small vessels, and Run and Ai are so small that the inset has to enlarge them to make them visible at all. The whole nutmeg supply of the world came from a group about thirty miles across.
[The 1606 Hondius map of the East Indies remains in the repository as 2026-09-02-hondius-east-indies-1606.jpg if you would rather show the period cartography here or add it as a second slide.]
Keay calls the regional network the country trade: an “infinitely complex web of subsidiary voyages” in pinnaces, prahus, and junks, often commanded but rarely crewed by Europeans. These smaller vessels delivered produce and intelligence from remote ports and shallow waters to Company factories and ocean-going fleets.
Aceh supplied political access, while the Susan loaded pepper at Priaman. Bantam functioned as the hub: large ships connected it to England, while regional vessels connected it to the Banda Islands, Moluccas, and other Asian ports. The network created commercial capability and an auditing problem. Keay writes that it “invariably confounded the auditors but enriched the adventurers.”
The subsidiary voyage dispatched from Bantam toward the Moluccas in early 1603 brought the English to Pulo Run. The regional network therefore generated the later territorial claim.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §iv. - Locator map generated by scripts/2026-09-02-eic-places-map.R; coastlines from the R maps package (CIA World Data Bank II).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The EIC did more than its charter mentioned
text:
The EIC did more than its charter mentioned


The charter created an English monopoly. EIC added diplomacy, armed seizure, and permanent foreign presence.


Timing: 73–75 minutes. Stop the timeline at 1603, the end of the first Company voyage.
Separate the authority granted in London from the capacities exercised abroad. The 1600 charter created an exclusive English trading organization with authority over its members and maritime conduct. Lancaster then negotiated with an Asian ruler, used armed force against Portuguese shipping, and left factors at a permanent trading agency.
None of these steps yet gave the Company authority to govern territory or populations. Ask which actions students nevertheless classified as imperial power. This preserves the distinction between imperial capacity and colonial rule and leaves the later transformation for the epilogue.
[Source] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §iii–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Run turned trade into a territorial commitment
text:
Run turned trade into a territorial commitment





Threatened by the Dutch, Run’s leaders offered allegiance to the English in 1616 (English protection in echagne for nutmeg access).
The Company’s charter gave it no power to hold territory. The EIC accepted on the king’s behalf.
Four years of Dutch blockade later, the Company wanted rid of the island (too costly to defend), but King refused



Trade created demands for protection, turning a commercial relationship into a claim to colonial rule.


Map of the Banda Islands, copied from a chart found in 1602 · Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain


Timing: 75–78 minutes. The pledge was sealed with a nutmeg seedling rooted in Run’s soil, which is worth telling aloud: seedlings were closely guarded and destroyed rather than surrendered, so handing one over was an act of real trust. Treat the pledge as a sovereign act by a self-governing polity choosing a protector under duress, after its neighbours had been coerced into Dutch control. Run places colonial rule on the table because the claim concerns territory, people, and governing authority.
Then the anticlimax, which is the honest ending. Keay: the island “never quite lived up to expectations” and “would become a fraught and expensive liability.” After a blockade lasting four years, the Company wanted to surrender Run. The Crown insisted on keeping “his exotic windfall and his Bandanese subjects.” The territorial prize was the authority the Company least wanted once it had it.
Close the loop on the activity: territorial authority belongs clearly in the imperial-power category and introduces colonial rule. The Company nevertheless tried to abandon Run when the territorial claim became a costly liability.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i. - Map of the Banda Islands, Nationaal Archief / Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The Company met each problem with organization or with force
text:
The Company met each problem with organization or with force







Cross-border problem
Company response




Portuguese and Dutch power restricted access
Charter, royal diplomacy, and armed ships


Voyages required capital and risk pooling
Capital subscribed one voyage at a time, then repaid when the ships returned


English exports found few Asian buyers
Bullion and country trade supplied tradable goods


Fleet arrivals distorted prices and delayed ships
Bantam factors traded year-round and prepared cargo




Timing: 81–84 minutes. Read each row from left to right and connect it to evidence already presented.
Portuguese and Dutch power restricted access to the spice trade. The English response combined an exclusive Crown charter, royal letters to Asian rulers, diplomacy at Aceh, and heavily armed ships. The 1600 charter created an English trading monopoly and internal Company government; it did not yet authorize territorial rule.
Long voyages required large amounts of capital and exposed investors to catastrophic loss. Subscriptions pooled capital for individual voyages, while centralized Company command organized the fleet. Permanent joint stock came later.
England made little that Southeast Asian markets wanted. Lancaster carried Spanish silver, seized Indian textiles, and exchanged those textiles for pepper. Country trade subsequently connected regional Asian markets and supplies.
Fleet arrivals simultaneously raised the price of spices the Company wanted to buy, lowered the price of the cloth it wanted to sell, and left ships waiting for cargo. Year-round factors spread transactions across time and prepared return cargo before the fleet arrived.
Distance made local knowledge indispensable but weakened oversight from London. Country trade extended the Company’s reach through Asian markets and carriers while increasing agent discretion and creating monitoring and auditing problems.
This is more precise than saying the Company simply internalized transactions. The EIC internalized selected coordinating functions while relying extensively on Asian merchants, carriers, rulers, and markets. Political authority was part of the organizational solution, not a separate contextual variable.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §ii–§iv. - Ronald H. Coase, “The Nature of the Firm,” Economica 4, no. 16 (1937): 386–405. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976).

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Epilogue: from Spice Race to Colonialism
text:
Epilogue: from Spice Race to Colonialism


Territorial revenue extraction made permanent military power self-financing.


Timing: 78–81 minutes. This is a contingent sequence, not an automatic evolution from factory to colony.
Permanent establishments created sunk assets and security commitments. Fortified settlements and European rivalry pulled Company agents into military competition and political alliances. In eighteenth-century India, the Company intervened in regional conflicts using Indian allies, financiers, intermediaries, and predominantly Indian sepoy armies.
The decisive transition was fiscal. Victories at Plassey in 1757 and Buxar in 1764 preceded the 1765 grant of the diwani, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. The Company could now use territorial taxation to finance permanent military power. Revenue funded armies; armies secured additional territory and revenue. The trading company became a military-fiscal company state governing populations.
Financial crisis, corruption, and administrative failure brought the British state further inside Company government. The Regulating Act of 1773 and Pitt’s India Act of 1784 imposed increasing parliamentary supervision. After the rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 transferred the Company’s territories, revenues, armies, and administrative powers to the Crown. That was the transition from Company colonialism to Crown colonialism, not the beginning of colonialism.
The VOC demonstrates that the path could unfold earlier and differently. Its destruction of Jayakarta and creation of Batavia in 1619, followed by the conquest of Banda in 1621, converted chartered commercial powers into colonial coercion in the spice-producing islands. The English Company’s path in India took longer and turned on control of territorial revenue.
[Sources] - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, §i–iv. - Philip J. Stern, The Company-State: Corporate Sovereignty and the Early Modern Foundations of the British Empire in India (Oxford University Press, 2011). - UK Parliament, “Parliament and the East India Company.” - UK Parliament, “East India Company and Raj, 1785–1858.” - Rijksmuseum, “The Dutch East India Company (VOC).”

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: The EIC is an ancestor of the modern MNE
text:
The EIC is an ancestor of the modern MNE


Chartered company

Permanent factories placed Company agents and assets abroad
Charter, diplomacy, and armed force supported trade
Commercial activity generated claims over territory and people


Modern multinational

FDI creates a lasting interest and managerial influence abroad
Market access is governed by host-state law and trade and investment rules
Firms face political risk but normally lack sovereign authority



The continuity is organization across distance. Modern law more sharply separates corporate authority from sovereign power.


Timing: 84–86 minutes. Make a bounded comparison. The EIC belongs in the history of multinational organization because it pooled capital, coordinated distant agents, maintained overseas establishments, and operated across several markets. It is not a modern multinational in institutional form.
The Crown granted exclusive access to English merchants, sent letters to foreign rulers, and tolerated or authorized armed commercial action in wartime. Company activities generated claims to public authority, including Run’s pledge of allegiance. Later charters expanded the Company’s authority to hold and govern territory.
Modern multinational firms organize foreign affiliates through corporate law, ownership, contracts, and managerial hierarchy. Their access is structured by host-state law and international trade and investment rules. They bargain with governments and face political risk, but they do not normally possess legal authority to wage war, negotiate sovereign treaties, or govern populations.
The current IB lesson is therefore specific. Cross-border firms still solve problems of capital, information, local adaptation, and control. The EIC solved them through an institutional bundle that joined corporate and sovereign power much more closely than modern law ordinarily permits.
[Sources] - Keay, Chapter 1, §i–§iv. - Peter J. Buckley and Mark Casson, The Future of the Multinational Enterprise (Macmillan, 1976). - Jean J. Boddewyn and Thomas L. Brewer, “International-Business Political Behavior: New Theoretical Directions,” Academy of Management Review 19, no. 1 (1994): 119–143.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Reflection: Return to your IB Voice
text:
Reflection: Return to your IB Voice

Why did England organize Asian trade through a monopoly company rather than through competing merchants or direct Crown control?


Revisit your opening answer: explain what the charter solved and what new political problem it created.


Timing: 86–89 minutes. Return students to the claim they made at the beginning of class. Ask for one revision grounded in evidence from the lecture.
Strong answers should distinguish the merchants’ need for pooled capital, exclusivity, and sovereign backing from the Crown’s interest in English shipping capacity, strategic competition, and control over English participation. The cost of the bargain might include excluded merchants, the pressure of Court patronage, English rivals who traded in defiance of the monopoly, private coercion, or the later expansion of delegated authority.
Do not require consensus about which side needed the other more. The purpose is to make students revise an initial causal judgment using evidence.
[Source] - Keay, Chapter 1, §ii–iv.

title: Trade, Coercion, and the EIC
section: Lessons learned this week
text:
Lessons learned this week


1. States carve out markets
The charter and the Canton system decided who could trade. Commerce then acquired armies and territory.
2. Open trade has losers, and they fight
Corn Laws Repeal enriched manufacturers and cost landowners. Dutch displacement led to embargo.
3. Institutions determine who wins
The same argument loses in a landowners’ Parliament and wins in 1846. A monopoly charter bestows market exclusivity.

4. Ideas need political translators
Smith/Ricardo defined the logic of trade. Cobden’s League and a famine shaped politics. Lancaster partied and shared the Queen’s letter.
5. Incentives for the illicit
Seized carracks, opium. Norms, law, and weapons imperfectly constrain.
6. State and commercial power reinforce each other
Commercial power extends state reach; state power protects commercial advantage.


Timing: 89–90 minutes. These are claims about how markets and political authority produce each other, not a summary of the narrative. Each one should be arguable.
On the first, the point is that the market did not exist prior to the authority that defined it. A charter, a Portuguese trading licence, and the Canton system are three different instruments for the same act: deciding who may trade, where, and with whom. The second sentence is the harder half. Once commerce holds a privilege it starts acquiring the means to defend it, so the Company accumulated armed shipping, treaty-making, and eventually territory and revenue. Commercial interest and coercive authority did not stay separate spheres that occasionally touched; they fused into a single organisation. Ask students where the line between firm and state actually falls in 1616, or in 1765.
On the second, resist the framing of free trade as efficiency against ignorance. Repeal moved income from landowners to manufacturers and to consumers of bread, and the losers understood that perfectly well, which is why they held it off for three decades. Every trade regime creates a distribution, and the fight is over who gets to set it. This is also the honest reading of Elizabeth’s letter: England argued for open trade where it was excluded and for monopoly where it was not.
On the third, the venue is not neutral. The same economic argument that persuades an economist fails in a Parliament elected on a franchise that over-represents landowners, and succeeds once the coalition and the crisis change. Institutions determine whose preferences get counted. The charter, Parliament, and the later Regulating and India Acts are all venues in which particular interests were advantaged by design.
On the fourth, ideas do not travel on their own merit. Smith and Ricardo supplied the analytical case decades before repeal, and nothing happened. What moved policy was Cobden’s organised campaign, the money and membership behind it, and then a famine that made the political cost of protection unbearable. Rhetoric, resources, and shock did the work that argument alone could not. Say plainly that this is not an argument that ideas are irrelevant, only that they are insufficient.
On the fifth, high returns pull activity toward whatever the law does not reach. Lancaster took a Portuguese carrack by force, Company servants ran the country trade partly on their own account, and private traders carried opium into a market that had banned it. In each case the profit was legal or illegal depending on which authority you asked. This is where norms and ethics enter the course rather than as a coda: the constraint on commercial behaviour is whatever combination of law, enforcement, and professional norm actually binds, and all three were weak at a distance of six months’ sail.
[Sources] - William J. Bernstein, A Splendid Exchange, Chapter 11. - John Keay, The Honourable Company, Chapter 1, “Islands of Spicerie.”
